title: Intussusception
subtitle: Enema reduction first, theatre when it fails or the child is sick

sources.org: American Pediatric Surgical Association (APSA) Outcomes and Evidence Based Practice Committee
sources.title: Management of intussusception in children: a systematic review (Kelley-Quon et al, J Pediatr Surg 2021;56(3):587-596)
Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: intussusception

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people in hospital (NG29)

red_flags.text: Peritonitis, free air, or shock that does not respond to resuscitation. These children go to theatre, not to the enema.
Lethargy or pallor out of proportion to the abdominal signs. Some infants present as an altered conscious level with no classic colic.
Redcurrant jelly stool and bilious vomiting are late signs that the bowel is already compromised. Their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
A child outside the usual age range (older than about three years), or with recurrent intussusception: look for a pathological lead point.

do_now.text: Intravenous access, bloods, and an isotonic crystalloid bolus at the NICE NG29 volume for any child with signs of shock, reassessing after each bolus.
Nasogastric tube on free drainage if vomiting or distended, and nil by mouth.
Inform the paediatric surgeon before the enema starts. The surgeon must be available on site during the reduction in case of perforation.
Stable child without peritonitis: proceed promptly to image-guided enema reduction. Delay increases the chance that reduction fails and that bowel becomes ischaemic.

assess.text: Classic history: episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of the legs, pallor, and quiet intervals. Ask about a recent viral illness.
Examine for a sausage-shaped mass, an empty right iliac fossa, distension and peritonism. Do a careful hydration assessment.
Look for lead-point clues: Henoch-Schonlein purpura, Peutz-Jeghers pigmentation, Meckel history, cystic fibrosis, lymphoma in an older child.

investigate.text: Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice in experienced hands: a target or doughnut sign, usually in the right abdomen.
Blood gas with lactate, electrolytes, full blood count, group and save.
Plain film only to look for free air or obstruction when perforation is suspected; it cannot exclude intussusception.
Small-bowel to small-bowel intussusception found incidentally on ultrasound is often transient. Re-scan rather than reduce if the child is well and it is short.

resuscitate.text: Restore circulating volume before the enema. A dry child tolerates a perforation far worse than a resuscitated one.
Adequate analgesia before and during the reduction; sedation per local radiology protocol.
Routine antibiotics before enema reduction are not needed in a stable child. Give them per local protocol when perforation or ischaemia is suspected, or before surgery.

definitive.text: Pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic enema under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance is first-line for the stable child without peritonitis.
If the first enema achieves partial reduction and the child remains stable, a delayed repeat enema may be attempted rather than proceeding straight to surgery.

Operate for failed reduction, perforation during the enema, peritonitis, or persistent instability. Laparoscopic reduction is often successful; convert when the bowel cannot be reduced or is non-viable.
At surgery, reduce by squeezing the apex back (milking proximally), never by pulling. Resect irreducible, gangrenous bowel or a pathological lead point.

escalate.text: Perforation during air enema can cause tension pneumoperitoneum with cardiorespiratory compromise. The team must be ready to decompress with a needle immediately.
No paediatric radiology or surgery on site: transfer after resuscitation, with a nasogastric tube and an escort.
Recurrence after successful reduction is common in the first days. Parents need clear advice to return early.

notes: Most intussusception in infants is idiopathic and ileocolic. In an older child, think lead point before you think idiopathic.
The enema is a procedure with a perforation risk, not a scan. It belongs in a setting where a surgeon can operate within minutes.
After successful enema reduction of an ileocolic intussusception, short observation and discharge is safe in selected children rather than routine admission.
